newsitem.title: USA: No CFTC, Treasury pact yet on retail derivatives.
newsitem.headline: No CFTC, Treasury pact yet on retail derivatives.

text.p: U.S. regulators have yet to agree on how to protect retail customers from fraud in foreign exchange derivatives transactions but have made progress in the past few weeks, Deputy Assistant Treasury Secretary Roger Anderson said Tuesday.

In testimony to a House Agriculture subcommitee looking at revisions to the basic U.S. futures-trading law, Anderson said Treasury believed retail customers deserved federal protection. Discussions were under way among Treasury, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission and banking agencies "to try to agree on a common level of protection," he said.
Treasury offered no proposal on "professional" markets that would be limited to experienced and well-financed participants.

As in Senate testimony, Anderson asked for retention of the 1974 Treasury amendment to the Commodities Exchange Act that exempted from CFTC control the off-exchange dealings in foreign currency, government securities and some other financial instruments.

While CFTC and Treasury do not agree on many points, they concur that CFTC should pursue retail fraud by entities not regulated by other federal agencies. That point is part of a Treasury proposal for legislative action.

The Treasury proposal also says dealings in government-securities derivatives should be exempt from the Commodity Exchange Act unless the transaction was conducted at a futures exchange and that over-the-counter institutional markets for foreign exchange derivatives are not subject to the CEA.
